articles.title: Amazon snaps up Decart’s AI optimization tech for $7.5B as it prepares to sell Trainium chips
articles.excerpt:
Amazon has agreed to acquire a good chunk of Israeli startup Decart.
The e-commerce and cloud giant is paying $7.5 billion for the startup, according to Bloomberg.
Decart has made a name for itself building interactive real-time world models — most recently Oasis 3 — and AI video generation tools. But under the hood, the company stands out for its Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), software that helps AI models to run efficiently on Nvidia, Amazon, and Google’s hardware.
As part of the deal, Amazon will acquire the technology behind DOS, as well as Decart’s founding team and team of AI researchers and engineers, Amazon said in a blog post.
“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, quantum computing, at Amazon. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”
Amazon, which has been so far been using its Trainium chips at its own data centers, is preparing to start selling them to customers as a competitor to Nvidia. Decart’s technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips, rather than Nvidia’s, which has been the gold standard so far.
Decart and Amazon did not immediately return requests for comment.
articles.summary: Amazon has agreed to acquire a good chunk of Israeli startup Decart. Decart’s technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips, rather than Nvidia’s, which has been the gold standard so far. Decart and Amazon did not immediately return requests for comment.

articles.title: Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
articles.excerpt:
Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
EVERGREEN, Colo. — Joan Spalding has driven the steep, winding road that leads to her house outside Denver for more than 50 years. But these days, the 89-year-old barely touches the steering wheel or the pedals.
Instead she tells the car where she wants to go, and presses a button on the large touch-screen in the dashboard of her Tesla Model Y.
"I just get in and go," Spalding says.
For all practical purposes, the car appears to be driving itself, navigating confidently on twisting roads through postcard valleys full of juniper and ponderosa pine.
"Now this is probably one of the narrowest roads," Spalding says, as the car pulls onto a dirt track that can barely fit two cars side by side, with a steep drop off to one side.
The Tesla handles the tight turns gracefully, even stopping to let an SUV squeeze by in the other lane.
Spalding was skeptical at first of what Tesla officially calls Full-Self Driving (Supervised), often abbreviated as FSD. It's a subscription service that drivers pay for, usually $99 dollars per month.
That was, until she saw what it could do.
"When I was driving," Spalding said, "I saw that the kind of things that it did were safer than what I would do."
There are more older drivers on the road than ever, and families often struggle with the question of when it's time to stop driving. Now, seniors are using emerging technology to stay behind the wheel longer, specifically automated systems made by Tesla. But safety experts worry the company may be over-selling what its cars can do.
"It's not a technology that I would drive with. It's not a technology that I would suggest that my loved ones use. I think it has a few safety gaps that just make me uncomfortable," said Bryan Reimer, a research scientist at MIT, who studies how drivers interact with technology.
It's hard to know exactly how many seniors are using Tesla's automated driving system, but the numbers may be growing. Overall, Tesla says FSD has more than 1.7 million active subscriptions, an increase of 67% from a year ago. If the car-maker knows how many of those subscribers are seniors, it isn't saying.
Riding along with Joan Spalding, it's easy to understand the appeal for older drivers. The car gives her mobility and freedom that she wouldn't have otherwise.
Before she got her Tesla, Spalding had gotten into a number of minor fender benders. Then, two years ago, she was in a serious crash while she was trying to make a left turn.
"I made a wrong decision. I wasn't focusing on what I should be doing … I was lucky," she said. "But I realized then that my abilities were not where I wanted them to be."
Her son Mike Spalding had known for a while that his mother's driving was getting worse. He was already driving a Tesla, and it was his idea to get one for her.
"It would be safer for mom if she was in a wreck because it's got all kinds of safety features. And then safer for people around her if we didn't have any more crashes. I've been driving one for years, and so I'd experimented with the Full Self-Driving and saw what it could do," Spalding said. "It's better than me."
Tesla agrees. The company claims that FSD is up to nine times safer than human driving. Tesla doesn't release much data about FSD, so it's impossible to independently verify whether its safety claims are true, Reimer said. He concedes Tesla's technology is impressive and is getting better all the time, but says it's not a replacement for a human driver — at least, not yet.
"Tesla has continually over-promised and under-delivered," Reimer said. "Full self-driving is not full self-driving, but yet the name feels so real."
If you read the fine print, FSD is not fully autonomous. The company always uses its full title — FSD (Supervised) — in official communications, to underscore the point. The driver is supposed to be paying attention at all times, in case the car encounters a situation FSD can't handle.
The problem, according to safety experts, is that human drivers tend to get complacent.
"It's good enough, often enough, where people go, 'The next time I'm in this similar situation, I know how it's going to behave,'" said Alexandra Mueller, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, the nonprofit funded by the insurance industry.
But Mueller worries older drivers won't be ready or able to take control of the car in an emergency.
"This can be a huge problem," she said. "Ultimately it is very unsafe if you have drivers who are not fully competent due to age-related impairments or decline."
Tesla did not reply to requests for comment.
The company has not said exactly how many senior drivers are using FSD to stay on the road longer, or even if that's something Tesla is tracking. But the company's CEO, Elon Musk, has encouraged the practice.
In a recent post on his social media platform X, Musk said that "Tesla self-driving gives mobility to seniors." Several times, he's amplified a video from a YouTube channel called TFLEV, featuring a 98-year-old man, who just bought his first Tesla.
"It has not made a mistake. And I've been driving it probably two or three months and it's not made an error in its driving, " the driver, Larry Dimmock, said in the video. "In fact, the other day it stopped. A chipmunk was crossing the road and there was no other traffic and it did not run over the chipmunk."
Musk reposted the video last month, saying, "At Tesla, we even care about the chipmunks." The clip has been viewed more than 3.5 million times.
"My moment of fame, I guess," Dimmock joked in an interview with NPR.
Dimmock says he's owned dozens of cars in his life, starting with a Ford Model A. He says he's still a pretty good driver at 98 — but not as good as his Tesla.
"I feel safer riding with this auto system than I do driving or riding with anybody. It's just been flawless," Dimmock said. "I'll get in the car and go somewhere, otherwise, I probably wouldn't."
For Joan Spalding in Colorado, it's more than just a question of convenience. She says FSD is allowing her to live independently in the house that she and her late husband built more than 50 years ago.
"I love the solitude of being in that place and being by myself," she said.
Without the mobility that FSD gives her, Spalding said, she would likely have to find another place to live where she wouldn't need to drive.
"I'd have to move," she said. "This way, I think I can drive it for as long as I want to. I don't see any reason why not."
articles.summary:
Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
EVERGREEN, Colo. Spalding was skeptical at first of what Tesla officially calls Full-Self Driving (Supervised), often abbreviated as FSD. It's hard to know exactly how many seniors are using Tesla's automated driving system, but the numbers may be growing.

articles.title: An Open Letter Offering Jensen Huang Free Use of PhantaField's Technology
articles.excerpt:
Dear Jensen,
We offer you the use of every technology PhantaField owns, free of charge. If something we’ve built can help you make the next generation of chips, we’d be glad to share it with you.
Professor Chenming Hu showed us what it means to move Moore’s law forward. He and his colleagues shaped a transistor’s channel into a thin fin so the gate could control the current from several sides. His work helped the industry scale from the 28 nm node to the 3 nm node and laid the groundwork for today’s NVIDIA chips. We’re following in his footsteps as we work to advance Moore’s law beyond 7 Å. In November 2023, he became PhantaField’s first investor.
We started by building a tool. Professor Hu’s investment helped fund our 300 mm tool, NanoGalaxy. It uses metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD), assisted by plasma and ultraviolet light, to grow 2D TMD semiconductor films a few atoms thick. The growth temperature is low enough for the circuits already on the wafer. The new film can then be patterned into another layer of CMOS transistors.
Our Van der Waals 3D DRAM design uses those layers for memory. Each cell uses two transistors to store and read a bit without a separate capacitor. Stacking the cells adds memory within the same chip footprint. A chipmaker could put a memory die beside a GPU, bond memory tiles underneath it, or grow memory directly on the processor wafer.
Sophon brings arithmetic into the stack. In our AI processor design, 32 memory layers alternate with 32 logic layers. A model weight can travel from its memory cell to the circuit directly beneath it for multiplication. The memory barrier is gone, and the chip can do more work with less energy.
White Matter addresses a problem we face when we put many chips together. How do we cool the dies in the middle? Our package design eliminates the need for a printed circuit board or a heavy copper block. Everything sits on a silicon interposer with channels etched into it for liquid coolant. The resulting block of silicon can fit three racks’ worth of chips into a space half the size of a shoebox.
As data center construction faces tighter restrictions in the United States, we believe Sophon and White Matter offer the best solution for computing in space. We estimate that the cost per token in orbit would be half that of a land-based data center. Our 2D TMD transistors are also more resistant to radiation than conventional transistors, so Sophon can run in orbit without the heavy shielding that a GPU needs. Our 2T0C memory cells are less likely to lose their contents in a radiation event, so Sophon can keep working when a GPU would have to stop and retry.
Seer glasses bring the idea home. Our 2D TMD semiconductors enable a transparent display on the lens. In our design, a customized Sophon in the Pylon station would run a personal AI and render what the wearer sees. We envision a new form of personal computing in which we can cast a spell in our own virtual universe and see it come to life.
Jensen, if you have time to sit down with us in Santa Clara, we’d be glad to show you what we’ve built and how it works. Whatever you choose to do, you’ll have our full support and free use of our technology.
With respect,
The PhantaField team
articles.summary: Our Van der Waals 3D DRAM design uses those layers for memory. A chipmaker could put a memory die beside a GPU, bond memory tiles underneath it, or grow memory directly on the processor wafer. In our AI processor design, 32 memory layers alternate with 32 logic layers.

articles.title: Include partners with Altex Romania, delivers smart city technology in Pecica
articles.excerpt:
Include partners with Altex Romania, delivers smart city technology in Pecica
November 20th 2026
    
   Include has signed a distribution agreement with Altex Romania, the countryâs leading electronics and IT retailer, to support the deployment of Includeâs smart city technology in Romania. With more than three decades in business, Altex has an established nationwide presence. Its B2B division also provides technology solutions to businesses and public institutions.
The first project under the partnership was completed in August 2026, with 80 solar-powered units installed in Pecica, western Romania. Each unit combines a smart bench with device charging, a public Wi-Fi hotspot and integrated air-quality sensors. Include adapted its existing technology to the projectâs requirements, bringing these functions together in a solution developed for the city.
The units are installed in parks, a public square, school grounds and other community spaces. They provide residents and visitors with access to charging and connectivity while adding new points for monitoring local air quality. The municipal project was financed through Romaniaâs National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).
Pecica illustrates how Includeâs technology can be integrated into wider urban infrastructure projects. This approach combines our experience in metal construction production, electronics, sensors and software with the requirements of local partners. We thank Altex and the City of Pecica for their cooperation on the project. We look forward to strengthening the partnership in 2027 and pursuing further applications of Includeâs technology in Romania.
—

articles.title: New report documents authoritarian use of technology across the globe
articles.excerpt:
New report documents authoritarian use of technology across the globe
Privacy International's latest report documents how states are deploying authoritarian technology to stifle dissent, assert control and diminish human rights. The report conveys how surveillance technologies are being expanded and entrenched with the purpose of exerting control over entire populations and/or specific groups of people such as journalists and human rights defenders.
What is the authoritarian use of technology?
EDRi-member Privacy International (PI) have been observing and monitoring an increase in states’ adoption of authoritarian practices and policies. These practices are facilitated by new and emerging technologies or embodied in their very deployment to stifle dissent, assert control and diminish human rights. These digital technologies, such as facial recognition, social media monitoring, spyware, and more, are being deployed — both online and offline — by authoritarian and democratic regimes alike. PI have coined the term ‘authoritarian use of technology’ to describe this global phenomenon.
PI believes that the authoritarian use of technology goes beyond the unlawful use or abuse of technologies by states that the organisation has been monitoring and exposing for years. Authoritarian use of tech results in a systematic undermining of democratic principles, erosion of the rule of law, exertion of significant social and political control, or normalisation of the surveillance of individuals and their communities – particularly those already at risk.
These technologies are being expanded and entrenched with the purpose of exerting control over entire populations and groups of people at risk, such as human rights defenders (HRDs), journalists, lawyers, activists, dissidents and those from minority ethnic, national and religious backgrounds. This is being done to target, persecute or ostracise them. This ultimately creates a ‘chilling effect’, spreading a fear of reprisal, which serves not only to infringe upon the rights of certain individuals, but of whole communities and populations. In turn, this has a corrosive effect on democratic institutions, mechanisms of accountability, oversight and redress, and the fabric of open societies.
What technologies are being deployed?
In their new report, PI examine the use of five technologies: facial recognition technology, mobile phone extraction, spyware, social media and intelligence monitoring, and mass communications surveillance. The report also provides several cross-cutting themes emerging from the authoritarian use of these technologies on human rights. These include: a systemic interference with the right to privacy, the erosion of and chilling effect on enjoyment of broader fundamental rights and freedoms, the disproportionate or discriminatory targeting of certain groups in society, the absence of clear legal basis, effective safeguards, and independent oversight, and lastly, the lack of accountability of private sector actors.
Facial recognition technology (FRT) is a technology that uses a camera to capture images of people’s faces and then extracts and processes their biometric data to verify an individual or identify a match against an existing image. The report collates examples of how governments and law enforcement are deploying FRT at protests to identify, monitor and track protesters either openly or surreptitiously, and even banning wearing face coverings at protests to facilitate it. The report also features case studies of FRT projects in the UK, Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territories, and Brazil.
PI’s report includes a chapter on mobile phone extraction, which documents the technology being deployed to gather information and intelligence about activists, journalists, political dissidents, and migrants, which they believe to constitute an authoritarian use of the technology. Our electronic devices, such as our mobile phones and tablets, contain huge amounts of information and sensitive data about our lives. Mobile phone extraction involves extracting data from an individual’s device, or from the cloud services they use, including device information, photos, videos, audio recordings, notes, documents and apps used, as well as the messages, call logs and emails they draft, send and receive.
The report also gathers examples of spyware repeatedly being deployed by both authoritarian and democratic governments to conduct secret, intrusive surveillance of journalists, human rights defenders, opposition politicians, their family members and other individuals already at risk of state repression. Spyware is a huge intrusive surveillance technology that can secretly get everything from a person’s phone: messages, photos, contacts, location, microphone, camera, and browsing history, without them ever knowing. The report refers to the NSO Group and The Pegasus Scandal, and examples from across the Gulf countries of Bahrain, United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.
The report also includes social media intelligence monitoring as a tool increasingly being used by governments and non-state actors for exercising authoritarian control. It draws on the US Department of State’s screening and vetting process of student visa applicants to include applicants’ social media, as well as its use to monitor and track government dissent and protestors in Colombia, the UK and Mexico.
Lastly, PI’s report covers the use of mass communications interception as posing one of the most significant intrusions for privacy, as it can be directed not just at specific individuals but at entire populations. Communications interception is the monitoring, interception, collection, preservation and retention of information that has been communicated, relayed or generated over communications networks by a third party such as law enforcement agency, intelligence agency, a private company, or a malicious actor. The report explains how International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) catchers, which function by mimicking nearby mobile cell towers and intercept communications and location data transmitted by personal communication devices, are being used to intercept protester’s communications and devices in the USA and allegedly the UK. The use of Bulk Communications Interception in Libya provides another example of what may be referred to as an authoritarian use of tech.
How can the authoritarian use of tech be curtailed?
Across their analysis of states’ deployment of such technologies, PI found that legislative, technical and regulatory safeguards to oversee the deployment of such technologies were weak, incomplete, unenforced, lacking entirely, or even explicitly serving to bolster and uphold their weaponisation as tools of oppression. Therefore, they conclude each chapter with a specific set of safeguards and restrictions pertaining to each technology that are required to restrict their use to ways that comply with human rights law. However, PI also concludes that certain technologies are so inherently intrusive by design that they are incapable of being reconciled with human rights standards. In particular, they believe that live FRT and mass communications interception exemplify this category of disproportionately intrusive technologies.
Conclusions
The collated case studies and examples of how these technologies are being used illustrates that these are not isolated incidents but part of a wider emerging global trend – the rise of the authoritarian use of technology as a phenomenon that is cutting across borders, cultures and jurisdictions.
PI will continue to monitor developments and raise awareness about the intrusive and devastating impact that the authoritarian use of technology can have on the enjoyment of human rights. They will continue to advocate for the necessary safeguards and restrictions that should be implemented to ensure states do not misuse and abuse these technologies.
Contribution by: Sarah Simms, Senior Policy Officer, Privacy International
articles.summary:
New report documents authoritarian use of technology across the globe
Privacy International's latest report documents how states are deploying authoritarian technology to stifle dissent, assert control and diminish human rights. What is the authoritarian use of technology? PI have coined the term ‘authoritarian use of technology’ to describe this global phenomenon.
